questions.question: A car's speedometer needle points to 60 kilometres per hour as the car passes a farm gate on a country road. What does that reading tell about the car?
questions.answer: How fast it is going at that moment
choices: How fast it is going at that moment
Its average speed since it set off
Its speed and the direction it is heading
How quickly its speed is going up
questions.context: A speedometer shows instantaneous speed, the speed at one moment. It shows no direction, so it is not a velocity, and it is not the trip's average speed, which is the whole distance divided by the whole time; how quickly the speed changes is acceleration.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade motion lessons set the speed shown at one moment (instantaneous speed, read off a speedometer) beside the average speed for a whole trip.

questions.question: A girl cycles to her grandmother's house. Whenever she is moving, her bike's speedometer reads 20 kilometres per hour, but halfway there she stops for a half-hour rest. How does her average speed for the whole trip compare with 20 kilometres per hour?
questions.answer: Lower, since the rest adds time but no distance
choices: Lower, since the rest adds time but no distance
Lower, since the rest shortens the distance ridden
The same, since stops are left out of an average
The same, since she always rides at that speed
questions.context: Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time, and the half hour of rest counts in the time. The road to her grandmother's house is just as long either way, so the rest pulls her average below the 20 kilometres per hour her speedometer showed while she rode.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards (TEKS 7.7A) have students work out average speed as total distance over total time, stops included.

questions.question: A radio weather report says only that a storm is moving at 30 kilometres per hour. A science teacher listening points out that the report has given the storm's speed, but not its velocity. What has the report left out?
questions.answer: Which way the storm is heading
choices: Which way the storm is heading
How long the storm has been moving
How far the storm has travelled
Whether the storm is speeding up
questions.context: Velocity is speed with a direction, so 30 kilometres per hour toward the east is a velocity. For a town nearby, the direction decides whether the storm arrives at all. How long it has moved and how far it has come are not part of velocity, and a change of speed is acceleration.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade (TEKS 7.7B) teaches velocity as speed with a direction and asks students to tell the two apart.

questions.question: A runner runs one lap of a 400-metre oval track in 80 seconds, finishing on the line she started from. Her average speed for the lap is 5 metres per second. What is her average velocity for the lap?
questions.answer: Zero, since her displacement is zero
choices: Zero, since her displacement is zero
5 metres per second, the same as her speed
5 metres per second, the way she ran
Unknown, since her direction kept changing
questions.context: Average velocity uses displacement, the straight-line change of position from start to finish, and a full lap ends where it began, so both are zero. Her average speed uses the whole 400 metres of path, so it is 5 metres per second even though her average velocity is zero.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade (TEKS 7.7B) teaches distance against displacement, and the lap that ends where it began is the standard case.

questions.question: Mia and Ben cycle away from the same gate at the same moment. On a distance-time graph, with distance up the side and time along the bottom, each ride makes a straight line, and Mia's rises more steeply than Ben's. What does the graph show?
choices: Mia rides faster than Ben
Mia rides more slowly than Ben
Mia rides up a steeper hill
Mia speeds up while Ben holds steady
questions.context: The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed: a steeper line gains more distance each second, so Mia is faster. The graph shows distance against time, not the shape of the road, and a straight line means each rider holds one steady speed.
questions.grade_note: Reading speed from the steepness of a distance-time graph is a seventh-grade standard (TEKS 7.7C).

questions.question: A boy walks from his house to a shop. On the distance-time graph of his trip, the line rises, then runs flat for five minutes, then rises again until he reaches the shop. What was he doing during the flat part?
choices: Standing still in one spot
Walking at one steady speed
Walking along level ground
Walking back toward his house
questions.context: A flat line on a distance-time graph means time passes while the distance stays the same, so he was not moving. A flat line means a steady speed only on a speed-time graph, and a distance-time graph shows nothing about whether the ground is level.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards (TEKS 7.7C) teach that a flat stretch of a distance-time graph means the object has stopped.

questions.question: A tram's distance-time graph for one minute of its run starts as a steep line, then curves over, growing less and less steep as the minute goes on. What does the curve show about the tram?
choices: It is slowing down
It is speeding up
It holds one steady speed
It is coming over a hill
questions.context: The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed, so a line growing less steep shows the tram covering less distance each second. The line still rises because the tram is still moving forward, and its curve shows how the speed changes, not the shape of the ground.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade graph reading (TEKS 7.7C) includes telling speeding up from slowing down by how a distance-time line bends.

questions.question: Two runners race down a track. On a graph of distance from the start line against time, each runner makes a straight line, and partway through the race the two lines cross. What is true of the runners at that moment?
questions.answer: They are level with each other
choices: They are level with each other
They are running at the same speed
They are both speeding up
They are both slowing down
questions.context: Where the lines cross, both runners are the same distance from the start at the same time, so they are side by side. Their speeds are the slopes, and two straight lines that cross have different slopes, so the runner with the steeper line is passing the other; straight lines also mean neither is speeding up or slowing down.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade distance-time graphs (TEKS 7.7C) compare two trips on one graph, and the crossing point is the classic place where students mistake same position for same speed.

questions.question: A car takes a long, curving bend at a steady 50 kilometres per hour, and its speedometer needle never moves. Is the car accelerating as it goes round the bend?
questions.answer: Yes, since its direction keeps changing
choices: Yes, since its direction keeps changing
Yes, since anything moving is accelerating
No, since its speed stays the same
No, since only speeding up counts
questions.context: Acceleration is any change in velocity, and velocity includes direction, so a car turning at a steady speed accelerates all the way round the bend. In everyday speech to accelerate means to speed up, but in science slowing down and turning count too, while a car holding one speed in a straight line is not accelerating at all.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade motion units define acceleration as any change in speed or direction, with the turning car as the standard example.

questions.question: Students in a science class sort moving things into two groups: accelerating and not accelerating. Which of these four belongs in the group that is not accelerating?
questions.answer: A train at one speed on a straight track
choices: A train at one speed on a straight track
A bus braking as it nears a bus stop
A skater gliding round a rink at one speed
A cyclist pedalling faster down a lane
questions.context: Acceleration is any change in velocity: speeding up, slowing down or turning. Only the train keeps both its speed and its direction the same; the braking bus is slowing, the cyclist is speeding up, and the skater is turning, which counts even at one speed.
questions.grade_note: Classifying motions as accelerating or not, with slowing down and turning both counted, is how seventh grade applies the definition of acceleration.
